claims.text: Within single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and their subsets, increasing the number of constituents lowers intrinsic stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy favors deformation twinning over conventional dislocation glide.
Twin-assisted deformation enhances yield strength.
Twin-assisted deformation enhances the work-hardening rate.
The proposed twin-assisted mechanism improves cost-performance relative to alloys with fewer constituents.
Stacking-fault energy governs the relative ease of twin formation versus dislocation glide.
The higher chemical complexity of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produces lower stacking-fault energy than in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes deformation-twin formation.
Deformation twins act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The barrier effect of deformation twins increases work hardening.
The barrier effect of deformation twins increases yield strength.
Reduced-component alloys predominantly deform by dislocation glide without significant twinning because they have higher stacking-fault energy.
Predominantly glide-mediated deformation in reduced-component alloys results in lower strain hardening.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, the quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit measurably higher stacking-fault energy under matched test conditions.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, the quaternary and ternary alloys will form fewer deformation twins.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-hardening rates.
Relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, the quaternary and ternary alloys will undergo plastic instability earlier.
The proposed relationships apply to the studied single-phase FCC alloys between 77 K and 300 K under controlled processing and strain-rate conditions.
Short-range order may contribute to the observed mechanical-property differences.
Lattice-distortion effects may contribute to the observed mechanical-property differences.
